title: Russian Missile Hits Poland During Allied Drills, Hegseth Restricts US-Canada Defense Ties, and SEC Probes Nvidia Accounting
subhead: A Russian missile and suspected drone landed in Poland as European forces trained nearby for post-war security, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth moved to curb US-Canada military cooperation and the SEC opened an accounting inquiry into Nvidia amid a sharp AI stock sell-off.

sections.heading: Russian Missile Strikes Polish Territory During Allied Drills; Denmark Expels Diplomat
sections.body:
Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in southeastern Poland on Friday during allied military exercises near the border, prompting Prime Minister Donald Tusk to condemn the incident as a deliberate provocation from Moscow, BBC and SCMP report. No casualties or structural damage were reported, though Warsaw warned that the timing coincided with European troop drills aimed at preparing a potential post-war mission in Ukraine.

Separately, Al Jazeera and the Wall Street Journal report that Denmark expelled a Russian diplomat after accusing Moscow of plotting with a banned local gang to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper in Copenhagen, an allegation Russia dismissed as lacking evidence. Meanwhile, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Russian leader Vladimir Putin a 'killer' in response to US President Donald Trump describing Putin as his 'friend', while CNA and Anadolu Agency report that Australia, Canada, and New Zealand jointly urged Moscow to accept a permanent, unconditional ceasefire.
sections.whyItMatters: Russian projectiles hitting NATO territory during allied exercises raise escalation risks along Europe's eastern flank even as Washington signals warmer bilateral ties with Moscow.

sections.heading: Pentagon Restricts US-Canada Military Ties as Watchdog Audits Defense Start-Ups
sections.body:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued a classified memo imposing new limits on the bilateral military relationship with Canada, escalating diplomatic friction between Washington and Ottawa, according to The Washington Post, Reuters, and Anadolu Agency. The directive adds operational strain to North American defense integration at a time when allied air and maritime coordination is under heightened scrutiny.

In Washington, The Washington Post also reports that the Pentagon's internal watchdog has launched an audit into defense contracts awarded to tech start-ups after reporting revealed that firms linked to President Trump's sons won major agreements. Separately, The Wall Street Journal reports that a classified US intelligence network experienced an operational outage, according to US officials.
sections.whyItMatters: Restricting defense cooperation with a core NORAD partner weakens continental deterrence, while the Pentagon inspector general audit puts defense procurement oversight under renewed congressional focus.

sections.heading: SEC Probes Nvidia Accounting as AI Sell-Off Erases Nasdaq 2026 Gains
sections.body:
The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices following questions over questionable chip sales in Asia and the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang, The New York Times and Wall Street Journal report. Despite the probe, President Trump publicly called on Nvidia to give Huang a 'second chance' and reinstate him, CNA and Al Jazeera note, while SCMP reports that US lawmakers released licensing records showing Washington had approved nearly 880,000 advanced AI chips for Chinese firms earlier this year.

On Wall Street, CNBC and AP News report that the S&P 500 and Dow Jones entered correction territory while the Nasdaq Composite erased all of its 2026 gains, as post-IPO declines in Anthropic shares failed to halt a broader sell-off across AI and semiconductor equities.
sections.whyItMatters: Regulatory scrutiny of Nvidia's Asian sales and a market-wide reversal in AI valuations signal that geopolitical export loopholes and capital spending doubts are colliding on Wall Street.

sections.heading: Vietnam Scraps Death Penalty for Drug Trafficking as COP31 Talks Stall
sections.body:
Vietnam's National Assembly passed a revised penal code on November 20 abolishing capital punishment for drug trafficking and narrowing the death penalty to only four offenses: treason, murder, terrorism, and illegal drug production, CNA reports. The legislative overhaul marks a major shift in Southeast Asian criminal justice policy and aligns Hanoi closer with European trade partners.

Meanwhile, Al Jazeera reports that COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya have stalled beyond their scheduled close as participating governments struggle to reach consensus on fossil fuel transition language and climate finance commitments.
sections.whyItMatters: Vietnam's penal reform aligns its legal framework more closely with international trade partners, while the COP31 impasse underscores deepening divisions over who pays for the global energy transition.

sections.heading: Judge Approves $7 Billion Roundup Settlement; 6.8-Magnitude Quake Shakes Peru
sections.body:
A US federal judge approved a $7 billion nationwide class-action settlement over claims that Bayer's Roundup weedkiller caused non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a ruling expected to resolve tens of thousands of pending lawsuits, The New York Times and AFP report.

In South America, a strong earthquake measuring 6.8 to 6.9 magnitude struck Peru's Andean Junin region, sending residents into the streets in Lima, according to Reuters and Anadolu Agency, with no immediate reports of casualties or major structural damage. In the United States, a federal jury in California convicted a former Uber driver of federal arson charges for sparking the deadly 2025 Palisades Fire that killed 12 people in Los Angeles, NBC News and The Hill report.
sections.whyItMatters: The Roundup ruling removes a multi-year legal overhang for global agribusiness, while seismic activity in the Andes highlights ongoing infrastructure vulnerability across Latin America.

sections.heading: Voyager 1 Reaches 24-Light-Hour Milestone as Mercury X-Ray Telescope Opens Eyes
sections.body:
NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft has traveled 16.1 billion miles from Earth, becoming the first human-made object so distant that radio signals traveling at the speed of light require a full 24 hours to reach it, Science Daily reports.

In parallel, Science Daily reports that a groundbreaking X-ray telescope en route to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations after eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, performing above scientists' pre-launch expectations. Separately, researchers reported new findings suggesting microplastics may pose greater biological risks than simple tissue accumulation.
sections.whyItMatters: Deep-space milestones from Voyager 1 and the Mercury X-ray mission demonstrate the durability of long-horizon space instrumentation despite tightening terrestrial science budgets.

bottomLine: A Russian missile strike on Polish territory during allied exercises and new US restrictions on military ties with Canada underscore mounting strain across Western alliances, even as an SEC accounting probe into Nvidia and a sharp AI stock sell-off wipe out Nasdaq's 2026 gains.
sources: BBC, SCMP, Al Jazeera, Wall Street Journal, CNA, Anadolu Agency, Washington Post, Reuters, New York Times, CNBC, AP News, AFP, NBC News, The Hill, Science Daily
